html:
The Samanid Empire was a Persian Sunni Muslim state ruled from Bukhara, which governed Transoxiana and Khorasan, in today's Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, Afghanistan and northeastern Iran, from 819 to 999.

The family came from Iranian landowning gentry. In 819 four Samanid brothers became governors for the Abbasid Caliphate. Their grandson Ismail Samani united their lands in 892 and made the dynasty independent in all but name. His tomb in Bukhara, a small domed brick building, still stands.

The Samanid court is why Persian survived as a great written language after the Arab conquest. They used Arabic for religion and science but wrote poetry and history in New Persian, in Arabic letters.

  • The poet Rudaki served at their court and is called the father of Persian poetry.
  • Ferdowsi began the Shahnameh, the Persian national epic, under Samanid rule.
  • The young Avicenna used the royal library at Bukhara.

Bukhara and Samarkand grew rich on trade in slaves, silver and paper. Samanid silver coins have been dug up in great numbers in Russia and Scandinavia, carried north by the fur trade.

From the mid 10th century Turkic slave soldiers held real power. In 999 the Turkic Kara-Khanids took Bukhara, and the Ghaznavids, founded by former Samanid soldiers, took Khorasan. The Persianate court culture the Samanids built was passed on to these Turkic rulers.
sum: The Samanid Empire was a Persian Sunni Muslim state ruled from Bukhara, which governed Transoxiana and Khorasan, in today's Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, Afghanistan and northeastern Iran, from 819 to 999.
